title: The dress rehearsal, and the side you are handed
summary: Run the whole format end to end on a side you did not choose, score your own ballot, adopt exactly one fix and take that speech again.
materials: the 2 minute and 1 minute sand timers, and the call bell
a sheet turned landscape for the flow, ruled the way week 3 taught it
a ballot sheet, ruled by hand, the same four boxes as week 7
laptop with the AI, used with a grown-up in the room

steps.title: Everything exactly as it will be, including the part you would rather skip
steps.body:
A dress rehearsal is not a practice. A practice works on one piece. A rehearsal runs the whole thing in order, at full length, with the timers going and the ballot on the table, including the parts you would quietly leave out if nobody were watching. That is the point: the parts you would leave out are the ones that go wrong on the night.

So, all four speeches in the order week 1 set out. The opening speech, two minutes, building your case and nothing else. The minute of questions, both ways. The reply, ninety seconds, answering what was actually said. The last word, one minute, spent on the one thing you are winning.

One thing is different tonight, and it is the whole lesson. You do not choose your side. It is handed to you, and tonight you are against the motion.

Here is why that is not unfair. At the final, sides are drawn on the day. A case you have only ever argued when you happened to agree with it is a case that has never been tested, and you will not find out it is thin until you are standing up with it. So you write both cases at full strength, the way you have since week 7, and then you take the one you are given.

You are not rehearsing the final's own motion tonight, on purpose. Rehearse the shape, not the sentence. The final's motion gets your real cases, not your practice ones.

The one fix rule. After the round, score your own ballot, all four boxes, out loud. Then pick exactly one thing to change. Not five notes, one fix, chosen because it would have moved the last box. Then take that one speech again, with the fix in it, on the same timer. One fix landed beats five noticed, every time, and it is the last honest thing you can do to a case before the day itself.

And the question underneath tonight: should you ever argue for something you do not believe? It is not a trick question and there is a real argument on both sides. A lawyer defends people they may think are guilty, because a court where only the popular get defended is not a court. And there is such a thing as saying a thing you know to be false in a room that trusts you. Somewhere between those two is a line you are going to have to draw for yourself. Tonight you get to feel where it is, because for one hour you are standing on a side that may not be yours. Say what you actually think into the recording, and say whether the hour moved it.

steps.title: Both cases, the ballot, then the side arrives
steps.body:
Both cases first, before anybody says which one is yours. One sheet, two columns, and each column has to be able to win. Steelman rule standing: if your against column is a case only a fool would run, you have not written the against case, you have written a target.

Strongest for the motion: arguing a side you do not hold is how you find out whether your own side is any good, and how anyone accused of anything ever gets defended. You cannot know what your case is worth until somebody has genuinely tried to beat it, and sometimes that somebody has to be you.

Strongest against the motion: words in your mouth are yours. A person who can argue anything convincingly and does, in front of people who believe them, is doing something to those people, and being good at it is not a defence. Some arguments deserve to be made badly.

Write one full-strength sentence for each side. Then, before the round, say out loud which one you actually believe and put a small mark beside it. That mark matters tonight: you are arguing against, whichever way it points, and afterwards you get to say which it was and whether it felt different.

Rule the ballot before the first speech, the same four boxes as week 7. Who answered the other side's best point, and what did they actually say. Who backed a claim with something checkable, and what was it. Who was easier to follow, and where exactly did the other one lose you. Who won, and the one sentence why.

Then set the room up properly, because a rehearsal rehearses the room too. Timers where both sides can see them. Flow sheet ruled and blank. Grown-up in the room, running the timers, helping neither side. The AI takes the other side and gets told to argue it hard.
checklist: Both cases were written at full strength before the side was handed to me, and each one could win
I marked which side I actually believe, and then argued the one I was given
The ballot was ruled with all four boxes before the first speech, not after
The room was set up as it will be on the day: timers visible, flow blank, a grown-up running the clock and helping neither side

steps.title: Record it
steps.prompt: Record the whole round in one take if you can: the two minute opening, the minute of questions, the ninety second reply and the one minute last word, with the timers where the camera can hear them. Then hold the ballot up and read all four boxes out loud, including the last one, even if it goes against you. Name the one fix you chose and say which box made you choose it, then deliver that one speech again with the fix in it. Finish with tonight's question in your own words: should you ever argue for something you do not believe, and did arguing the side you were handed feel dishonest, or just hard?
